Maladaptive Strategies.value: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
Being alone in a room or building

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the reported trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations suggests a medical-trauma theme, while avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces suggests transport or confinement-related trauma. Those themes are not supported by the trigger or threat items, which instead center on interpersonal conflict, crying, and hypervigilant safety positioning.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the strategy node, the three avoidance items point to three different situational themes—medical settings, transport, and enclosed spaces—without corresponding support from memory, appraisal, or trigger content. This makes the strategy profile look internally diffuse rather than like a coherent set of coping responses for one trauma formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
issues.explanation: The profile is only partially coherent for childhood physical abuse. Arguments, crying, and conflict avoidance fit the trauma type, but the combination of a highly specific tactile-texture trigger with public transport avoidance and enclosed-space avoidance is difficult to link to this trauma history without any memory or appraisal content explaining that association.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the threat/strategy pattern, back-to-wall positioning and safe-seat seeking imply marked hypervigilance in public or interpersonal environments, which could plausibly connect to transport avoidance, but enclosed-space avoidance suggests a more circumscribed claustrophobic or situational fear that is not otherwise represented in the trigger set.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Threat and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly linked, and Maladaptive Strategies strongly feed Triggers. Avoiding conflict fits the trigger set (arguments, crying), but avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces target contexts not reflected by the listed triggers, making the node contents insufficiently aligned with the edge pattern.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is not well supported by the rest of the profile for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. The listed triggers are arguments, crying, and unexpected touch, and the threat items center on interpersonal vigilance and positioning in rooms. Public transport avoidance suggests a different trigger/threat context and is hard to link coherently to the other selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is not clearly connected to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe hypervigilance in shared spaces and interpersonal danger cues, while the triggers are interpersonal/emotional and tactile. Being alone as a primary avoidance target pulls toward a different clinical pattern unless there were accompanying abandonment or panic-related items, which are absent here.

Difficulty concentrating is a nonspecific PTSD symptom rather than a threat appraisal/perceived current danger item. Within this node, the other threat items specifically reflect situational safety behaviors and surveillance of the environment. This item does not fit the node's theme and weakens alignment with the formulation in which Threat is tightly linked to Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette:
Amir was eleven years old the first time he learned that the safest place in a room was the wall. His father’s hand had come across the dinner table without warning—not a slap, but a hard, flat strike to the side of Amir’s head that sent his vision white for a moment. The argument had been about nothing: a grade, a forgotten chore, a tone of voice Amir didn’t even remember using. What he remembered was the shock of being touched, the way his mother’s face crumpled as she tried not to cry, and the certainty that any moment of disagreement could turn into a blow. Over the years that followed, the pattern became as predictable as gravity. A raised voice meant flinch. A sudden hand near his shoulder meant freeze. And crying—whether his mother’s silent tears after an incident, or later, anyone else’s—meant something was terribly, dangerously wrong.

Now nineteen, married for just over a year, and working as an environmental scientist for a small consulting firm, Amir had built a life that looked steady from the outside. But the internal architecture of that life was entirely defensive. In the office he chose his desk second, after watching where his coworkers sat—always the corner desk with his back to the wall, his line of sight open to the door and every face that entered. When he met with clients, he arrived early to seat himself at the far end of the conference table, or positioned himself against a bookshelf. He had come to believe that he could read danger in a furrowed brow, a too-quick exhale, a gaze that lingered a half-second too long. This scanning had become automatic, almost exhausting, but letting it go felt like taking off a helmet in a war zone.

At home, his wife Leila had begun to notice that he left the room whenever she started to cry—whether from a sad movie or a stressful phone call. He never said why; he only knew that the sound of it made his chest tighten and his feet move toward the door. Arguments were worse. When he felt a disagreement coming, even about something small like whose turn it was to do the grocery shopping, Amir would go silent, agree too quickly, or physically leave the house. He had never told Leila that the last time he’d argued with his father, he’d ended up with a cracked rib. She only knew that her husband seemed to disappear whenever things got hard.

Avoiding people was simpler. He had no close friends at work, no one he met for coffee. He took his lunch at his desk or in his car, and he scheduled field sampling days so he could be alone in the wetlands he monitored, away from colleagues. But that solitude brought its own terror: being alone in an empty building or a quiet stretch of marsh made his skin prickle. He was certain that in an open, unguarded space, something could come at him from any direction. So he kept his phone on, kept his back to a tree when he stopped, and never stayed late at the office if he could help it.

The cost of these habits had become visible. His supervisor had noted that he seemed “hard to collaborate with” and had put him on solo projects. Leila had started sleeping on the far side of the bed after waking one night to find Amir rigid, his eyes open, his arm locked across his chest as though bracing for a blow. She had been reaching out to touch his shoulder—something he’d told her he hated, being touched without warning—and he had jerked away so violently he hit his head on the headboard.

What finally brought Amir to a therapist’s office was not a single crisis but a slow erosion. He was tired of scanning faces, of feeling safe only in corners, of watching his wife’s confusion turn into frustration. He wanted to believe that a disagreement could end without harm, that crying didn’t mean someone was about to be hurt, that he could sit in the middle of a room and still breathe. He came because he was afraid that if he didn’t learn a different way to live, he would lose the marriage he had fought to build—and because, for the first time in years, he was willing to let someone see the fear he carried.
